title: Comparing Few-Shot Prompting of GPT-4 LLMs with BERT Classifiers for Open-Response Assessment in Tutor Equity Training
venue: AAAI 2025 Workshop iRAISE (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether contemporary large language models can match or outperform a fine-tuned BERT classifier when grading nuanced open-ended learner responses in an educational training context. Specifically, the authors examine automated assessment of scenario-based, equity-focused tutoring lessons where responses are not simple right-or-wrong factual answers but depend on contextual judgment and explanation.

The study compares fine-tuned BERT with few-shot prompted GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo on four binary prediction tasks drawn from two online tutor-training lessons: avoiding unconscious assumptions and helping students manage inequity. The data come from 291 completed responses written by 243 undergraduate tutors in the northeastern United States, all training to become middle school tutors in a remote tutoring organization. Human coders labeled responses, and the models were evaluated with stratified 5-fold cross-validation using accuracy, F1, and AUC where applicable.

The main finding is that BERT consistently outperformed both GPT-based approaches across the four tasks, with the clearest advantage in overall average performance. The authors conclude that for this kind of nuanced educational assessment, fine-tuning a task-specific smaller model is more effective and more resource-efficient than relying on few-shot prompting of commercial GPT models. They also note that GPT performance was less consistent and that these results suggest limitations of prompt-only approaches for ill-defined educational tasks requiring contextual reasoning.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed workshop paper using a clear comparative cross-validation design, but it is not an RCT or QED and focuses on model benchmarking rather than learner outcomes. The evidence quality is therefore correlational/technical rather than causal in the K-12 sense.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong classifier performance differences, but these are not educational effect sizes on student learning or behavior. Its practical impact is promising for assessment infrastructure, yet the demonstrated impact on learners is indirect and untested.

interventions.use_case: automated open-response assessment of tutor equity-training answers using fine-tuned BERT and few-shot GPT classifiers to score responses as adequate or inadequate
few-shot prompted GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo used as comparison models for judging open-ended tutor training responses in scenario-based equity lessons

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that fine-tuned BERT outperformed few-shot prompted GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo on automated scoring of open responses in tutor equity training, while also being more resource-efficient and offline deployable. Across tasks, average performance was BERT accuracy=0.837, GPT-4o=0.726, and GPT-4 Turbo=0.549; BERT also achieved AUC values around 0.794-0.953 on its binary classification tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy, F1, and AUC for automated open-response classification
finding.study_size: n=243 students; 291 lesson completions; 243 human-annotated responses (79 + 164 for the two lessons)

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that offline fine-tuned BERT may be a more stable, cost-efficient institutional option than commercial GPT models for scalable assessment in tutor training. The authors argue this could support broader deployment of automated evaluation in educational organizations, though the paper does not test institutional outcomes directly.
finding.measure: Comparative model performance and resource-efficiency discussion for deployment feasibility
